explanation: Medicines for digestion and body chemistry: diabetes, obesity, reflux, nausea, bowel and liver problems, vitamins and minerals.
Mostly lower blood sugar in diabetes; some are also used for heart failure, chronic kidney disease or obesity.
Replace or add to the body's own insulin, the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into cells.
Start working quickly and last a few hours, covering the rise in blood sugar after meals.
Contain a quick and a slower insulin, so one injection covers a meal and gives longer background control.
Non-insulin medicines lowering blood sugar, mainly in type 2 diabetes; some also treat obesity, heart failure or kidney disease.
Blood sugar-lowering medicines other than insulin that fit none of the named groups, used mainly in type 2 diabetes.
Medicines that prevent clots, stop bleeding (as in hemophilia), treat anemia or other blood disorders, or supply fluids and nutrition.
Stop or prevent bleeding, for example in hemophilia, during surgery or when platelet counts are low.
Help blood clot to stop bleeding, for example by replacing missing clotting factors, boosting platelets or sealing surgical wounds.
Replace missing clotting proteins, or add a gene to make them, in hemophilia and other bleeding disorders.
Medicines for the heart and blood vessels: high blood pressure, heart failure, irregular heartbeat, chest pain and high cholesterol.
Lower high blood pressure, including in the lung arteries (pulmonary arterial hypertension).
Blood pressure-lowering medicines that fit none of the other named groups, including those for high pressure in the lung arteries.
Medicines lowering high blood pressure in other ways, fitting none of the named groups.
Make the kidneys remove more water or salt, easing fluid buildup (swelling), heart strain or high blood pressure.
Medicines that make the kidneys remove more water or salt but fit none of the named diuretic groups.
Block vasopressin, the hormone making the kidneys hold water, so they release more; used, for example, for low blood sodium.
Medicines that fight or prevent infections, mainly working throughout the body: antibiotics, antifungals, tuberculosis drugs, antivirals, antibodies and vaccines.
Kill or stop bacteria throughout the body; used for bacterial infections such as pneumonia and skin, urinary or bloodstream infections.
Antibiotics for use throughout the body that fit none of the main antibiotic families.
Antibiotics for use throughout the body that fit none of the other named groups at this level.
Block viruses from multiplying in the body; used e.g. for HIV, hepatitis B and C, herpes viruses and flu.
Act directly on viruses, blocking steps they need to multiply, e.g. in HIV, hepatitis, herpes or flu.
Fake building blocks that stop the virus copying its genes into DNA; used for HIV and hepatitis B.
Prepare the immune system to recognize and fight a germ, preventing the disease or making it milder.
Train the immune system to recognize disease-causing viruses, preventing the diseases they cause or making them milder.
Protect against flu; seasonal vaccines are updated yearly for new strains, others target pandemic or bird flu.
Protect against viral liver infections (hepatitis), such as hepatitis A and B.
Cancer medicines (chemotherapy, targeted and hormone therapy) and medicines that calm or boost immunity, e.g. for arthritis or transplants.
Medicines that kill cancer cells or stop them growing: chemotherapy, targeted drugs, antibodies, and cell and gene therapies.
Cancer medicines that fit none of the chemotherapy, kinase inhibitor or antibody groups, sorted into smaller subgroups.
Cancer treatments made of living cells or genes, e.g. a patient's own immune cells modified to attack the cancer.
Medicines that boost the immune system or blood cell production: growth factors, interferons, interleukins and others.
Medicines that boost the immune system or blood cell production: growth factors, interferons, interleukins and others.
Growth factors that make the bone marrow produce more white blood cells, e.g. when chemotherapy has lowered them.
Calm the immune system in autoimmune diseases, e.g. arthritis, psoriasis, bowel inflammation, multiple sclerosis, and to prevent transplant rejection.
Calm the immune system in autoimmune diseases, e.g. arthritis, psoriasis, bowel inflammation, multiple sclerosis, and to prevent transplant rejection.
Immune-calming medicines that act on specific parts of the immune system rather than suppressing it broadly.
Block interleukins, immune messenger proteins that drive inflammation, or their receptors, calming overactive immune responses.
Lab-made antibodies that calm the immune system by attaching to specific targets, e.g. proteins on immune cells.
Medicines acting on the brain and nerves: anesthetics, painkillers, and medicines for epilepsy, Parkinson's, mental illness, dementia and addiction.
Medicines that prevent or reduce seizures in epilepsy by calming overactive electrical signaling in the brain.
Nervous system medicines that fit none of the main groups, including those for addiction or dizziness (vertigo).
Help people overcome addiction, for example to smoking, alcohol or opioids, often by easing cravings or withdrawal.
Treat opioid addiction, e.g. as substitutes that act on opioid receptors to ease withdrawal and cravings.
